cognate: Gk ἄμβροτος/ἀμβρόσιος = Ved. amŕ̥ta- (*n̥-mr̥-tó- 'immortal'); Gk ἕννυμι (ἕσσε, ἕσατο), εἷμα = Ved. vas- 'clothe' (vastām, vásāna-) (*wes-)
drift_or_renewal: Greek keeps 'immortal' as an adjective on the garment (ἄμβροτα εἵματα), Vedic has the substantivised neuter amŕ̥tam 'immortality, nectar' as the instrument one is clothed with; Greek has the matching substance noun ἀμβροσίη in the same line (χρῖσέν τ̓ ἀμβροσίῃ)
shared_syntax: transitive *wes- 'clothe' with a divine agent and a warrior's body as object, the 'immortal' element as garment/instrument: Gk περὶ δ̓ ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσε ~ Ved. sómas tvā rā́jā amŕ̥tena ánu vastām
context: A god clothes a warrior's body in 'immortal' stuff to protect it from death or decay. Il. 16.670/680: Zeus orders Apollo to wash dead Sarpedon, anoint him with ambrosia and clothe him in immortal garments; Od. 24.59 the Nereids do the same for Achilles. RV 6.75.18 = AVŚ 7.118.1, an armour spell: 'I cover your vital points with armour; let King Soma clothe you with immortality.' Il. 14.178 (Hera's ambrosial robe) and RV 2.10.1 (immortal Agni wearing splendour) show the same verb with 'immortal' outside the warrior setting. Wearing 'immortality' as a garment is a specific image, not a generic one, and in both traditions it belongs to protecting the hero's body.
phrase: *n̥mr̥tóm wes- 'to clothe (someone) in the immortal': Gk ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕννυσι ~ Ved. amŕ̥tena vaste

cognate: Gk ὠκύς = Ved. āśú- = Av. āsu- (*h₂ōḱú-); Gk ἵππος = Ved. áśva- = Av. aspa- (*h₁éḱwo-); Gk ζεύγνυμι, ζυγόν = Ved. yuj- (*yewg-)
drift_or_renewal: none for the core pair; Vedic often uses āśú- on its own for the yoked steeds (RV 1.118.4, 1.140.4); the chariot word differs (Gk ἅρμα vs Ved. rátha-)
shared_syntax: noun + epithet 'swift horses' as object or subject of 'yoke' (Gk ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν / ζεύξειεν ὑφ̓ ἅρμασιν ὠκέας ἵππους ~ Ved. ráthe yuktā́saḥ āśávaḥ, yujyante āśávaḥ); 'swifter/as swift as the wind' as the measure (AVP āśīyān aśva vātād ~ Il. 16.149 ἅμα πνοιῇσι πετέσθην)
context: Yoking chariot horses for a drive or race: Il. 23.294 the chariot race, Il. 16.148 Automedon yokes Xanthos and Balios, who 'fly with the winds', Il. 24.14 Achilles yokes his horses; RV 1.118.4 the Aśvins' swift birds yoked to the chariot, RV 1.140.4 wind-driven swift ones yoked, AVP 19.34.24 a race charm, 'be swifter than the wind, O horse, win the contest'. The same pairing appears in the Avestan compound āsu.aspa- 'having swift horses'.

cognate: Gk μέλι, -ιτος = Lat. mel, mellis (*mélit); Gk γλυκύς = Lat. dulcis (*dl̥kú-/*dléwkus)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic renews both words in the same figure: ghr̥tā́t svā́dīyo mádhunaś ca vocata 'speak (a song) sweeter than ghee and honey' (svādú- = Gk ἡδύς; mádhu = Gk μέθυ)
shared_syntax: comparative of 'sweet' with 'honey' as the standard of comparison (Gk gen. μέλιτος γλυκίων ~ Lat. abl. melle dulcior), also the plain epithet pair dulci melle
context: In Greek and Vedic the comparison describes speech or song (Il. 1.249: Nestor's voice flowing from his tongue 'sweeter than honey'; RV 8.24.20); in Lucretius 1.947 it is the poet's Muse-honey (musaeo dulci contingere melle); in Plautus it is an endearment; in Il. 18.109 it is anger. Caveat: these are the only native words for 'honey' and 'sweet' in Greek and Latin, and honey as the measure of sweetness is very common, so the match is weak evidence of inheritance. Plautus and Lucretius may also follow Greek models.
phrase: *mélitos dl̥kíyos 'sweeter than honey' (of speech or song)

cognate: Gk αἰών = Ved. ā́yus = Lat. aevum (*h₂éyu-/*h₂óyu-s 'life-force, lifetime')
drift_or_renewal: 'long' is renewed: Ved. dīrghá- (*dl̥h₁gʰó-, = Gk δολιχός) vs Gk δηρός (*dweh₂-ro-); Lat. dūrāre 'last', if it belongs with *dweh₂-ro- at all (more often derived from dūrus 'hard'), turns the adjective into a verb
shared_syntax: 'life(time)' + 'long' as predicate or object: Gk ἐπὶ δηρὸν δέ μοι αἰὼν ἔσσεται ~ Ved. dīrgham āyuṣ kṛṇotu 'may he make long life'
context: A long life-span, wished for or foretold: Achilles' choice in Il. 9.415, where a long aiōn at home is set against imperishable fame and opposed to the formulaic μινυνθάδιος αἰών 'short life'; the AVP verse is a wedding blessing (Tvaṣṭar give you a thousand lives, long life). The Lucretian 'last through the age' is only a loose echo.
phrase: *h₂óyus 'long' — 'long life' (Ved. dīrgham āyuḥ, Gk δηρὸν αἰών)

cognate: Gk δῶρον = ORuss/OCS даръ (*déh₃-ro-m 'gift'); Gk δίδωμι = ORuss дати (*deh₃-)
shared_syntax: figura etymologica: *deh₃- with its own -ro- noun as object (δῶρα δίδωσι ~ дасть ... дары)
context: A ruler hands over a lavish gift: Agamemnon's catalogue of gifts offered to Achilles (Il. 9.261), and the emperor's gifts of gold, silver, silks and vessels to Olga (Laurentian Chronicle). Weak: the -ro- noun is a shared Greek-Slavic(-Armenian) derivative, but any language with such a noun is likely to pair it with 'give' on its own.

cognate: Gk ἑάων (gen. pl. of ἐΰς 'good', as a noun 'goods') = Av. vaŋhu-/vohu- = Ved. vásu- (*h₁wésu-); Gk δίδωμι, δωτήρ = Ved. dā-, dātár- (*deh₃-)
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek and Vedic; Avestan dātar- is ambiguous between 'giver' (*deh₃-) and 'creator' (*dʰeh₁-)
shared_syntax: 'give' / 'giver' with the genitive plural 'of goods' (Gk δίδωσι ... ἑάων, δωτῆρες ἑάων ~ Ved. dātā́ vásūnām ~ Av. dāta vaŋhuuąm)
context: Il. 24.528: the two jars on Zeus' floor, 'of gifts such as he gives, one of evils, the other of goods' — a god as the giver of goods, as in Od. 8.325 θεοὶ δωτῆρες ἑάων, RV 8.51.5 (Indra) and Av. VS22.1 (Ahura Mazda). The anchor is weak: the slab's Avestan passage (fravashis) supplies only the cognate *h₁wésu- adjective, not the giving frame; the frame itself comes from the support witnesses.

note: All 277 bundles read. Most pairings are artefacts of the automatic root mapping: for example OE drēam/Av. druj-, OE fēower parsed as fe+wer, the repeated pairing of πότνια μήτηρ with AVŚ 7.6.3, and Greek prose partners. Two strong leads: clothing in the 'immortal' (Gk ἄμβροτα εἵματα ἕσσε ~ Ved. amŕ̥tena vastām) and swift horses yoked to the chariot. Rejected: the Av. pasu vīra merism (no cognate non-Iranian anchor in the slab; Od. 10.98 βοῶν/ἀνδρῶν renews both words), the *spend- libation (Il. 24.287 ~ Umbr. mefa spefa; lexical only), star similes, and κραδίη/cor + tremble (generic).
